classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the sum as groups with two distinct leadership roles, then reverse the count and recognise optional membership for the remaining n-2 students.

content.prompt:
A class has $n$ students. This time, a captain and a co-captain is chosen from the group formed.

By considering the number of possible groups that have a captain and a co-captain, show that
$$2\times1\binom{n}{2}+3\times2\binom{n}{3}+\cdots+n(n-1)\binom{n}{n}=n(n-1)2^{n-2}.$$

answer.short:
$2\times1\binom{n}{2}+3\times2\binom{n}{3}+\cdots+n(n-1)\binom{n}{n}=n(n-1)2^{n-2}$.

Count by group size, or choose the captain and co-captain first and let each remaining student join or stay out.
answer.worked:
For a group of size $k$, choose its members in $\binom{n}{k}$ ways. Choose the captain in $k$ ways and the co-captain in $k-1$ ways. There are $k(k-1)\binom{n}{k}$ outcomes. Adding the mutually exclusive cases $k=2,3,\ldots,n$ gives the left-hand side.

Alternatively, choose the captain in $n$ ways and the co-captain in $n-1$ ways. Each remaining student independently joins or stays out, giving $2^{n-2}$ membership choices. This gives $n(n-1)2^{n-2}$ outcomes.

Both methods count the same groups with their two distinct leadership roles, so
$$2\times1\binom{n}{2}+3\times2\binom{n}{3}+\cdots+n(n-1)\binom{n}{n}=n(n-1)2^{n-2}.$$
